blocks.text: My Practice
blocks.rawHtml: My Practice

blocks.text: Almost 30 years ago, I decided to focus my practice on working with more than one person, be it a partner, parents, or the whole family. I was also touched by folks who wanted to be in an intimate relationship but were instead feeling lonely and isolated.  The intimate connection that is engendered in individual therapy can be a very healing experience.  Also, Group therapy often seems like the right choice, as we can join with others in a family-type setting and create our own meaningful relationships in that context.

My hope is for each of us to explore our own deepest truths and express them in individual sessions, to our partners, our family or other group members, in a situation of being witnessed and supported.

blocks.text: About Me
blocks.rawHtml: About Me

blocks.text: I have been interested in psychology since I was about 10 years old. My dad was a psychoanalyst in New York City and his office was in our house. I saw his patients every day and was curious about what he did with them once they went into the office. It seemed like a mystery that people were being helped just by lying on a couch and talking.
blocks.rawHtml: I have been interested in psychology since I was about 10 years old. My dad was a psychoanalyst in New York City and his office was in our house. I saw his patients every day and was curious about what he did with them once they went into the office. It seemed like a mystery that people were being helped just by lying on a couch and talking.

blocks.text: As we grew up, my sister and I both took a strong interest in psychology and have both become clinical psychologists. So you might say, it was “all in the family”.  However, the idea of talking to someone one-on-one about their relationships with people who weren’t in the room, struck me as kind of strange.

blocks.text: Once in graduate school at the University of Rhode Island back in the early ’70s, I learned about something called Family Therapy where you saw the whole family at once. Then, instead of talking to someone about someone else, you could have the people talk to each other right in front of you. That made a lot more sense to me and turned out to be a lot more fun. And besides, it was exciting to do something so different from what my sister and father did.

blocks.text: In 1984, I began teaching Family Dynamics, Couples Therapy and Group Dynamics at the California Institute of Integral Studies in San Francisco, where I soon became a member of the Core Faculty. In my Family Dynamics class, the students brought in their families of origin and I worked with them doing family therapy right there in the classroom. We continued to do this with powerful results that cannot be called anything but transformational. In the couples class, students brought in their partners for an in-class session as well. In the Group Dynamics class, students would learn interactive skills, while getting feedback from their peers. I left C.I.I.S. in 2015, and am now Professor Emerita. It was an honor to be able to teach students my unique approach to family, couples and group psychotherapy. This is clearly my life's work.

blocks.text: My Qualifications
blocks.rawHtml: My Qualifications

blocks.text: My specialty is interpersonal communication, helping folks to talk to each other in a more direct and honest way. I have worked with couples, families, and groups for the last 40 years. I taught experiential classes in Family Dynamics, Couple Counseling, and Group Dynamics at the California Institute of Integral Studies in San Francisco since 1984, where I became a Full Professor and Core Faculty member. I am currently Professor Emerita. I have also taught these courses at John F. Kennedy University, Sofia University, Holy Names University, California State East Bay University and St. Marys College. I have had a private psychotherapy practice in Berkeley, CA since 1980 where I see couples, families, and individuals, and have facilitated groups for many years.

blocks.text: "Adult Children" and their Families
blocks.rawHtml: "Adult Children" and their Families

blocks.text: Despite all the good intentions that most parents have in raising us children, many of us still feel the wounds from our childhood, which can interfere with our hopes and dreams for how we want to live our lives. We may try to be a different kind of spouse or parent than what we saw modeled for us, but unconsciously, we may be holding onto ineffective patterns and acting them out in our new relationships and families.

We may try to be a different kind of spouse or parent than what we saw modeled for us, but unconsciously, we may be holding onto ineffective patterns and acting them out in our new relationships and families.

blocks.text: We carry our pain in the form of shame, low self-esteem, depression, anxiety, resentment, or just a lack of joy in our lives. Many of us seek out individual therapy to relieve ourselves from these unwanted burdens, but sometimes, until we meet with our original family of origin, these changes are very hard to make.

blocks.text: In my 30+ years of teaching Family Dynamics and Therapy at the California Institute of Integral Studies and many other bay area graduate programs, hundreds of students have brought in their families for in-class sessions, in an attempt to better understand their family’s dynamics and transform the roles they have all taken on for many years. It is remarkable to see how much transformation can occur in just one session.

blocks.text: Family therapy provides a unique opportunity to address these dynamics directly, in real time, with the people who are part of the system itself. Rather than working in isolation, family therapy brings together the voices, emotions, and perspectives of each family member, allowing for a more complete understanding of what is happening beneath the surface. In many cases, patterns that have existed for years—or even generations—can begin to shift when they are acknowledged openly in a supportive family therapy setting.

blocks.text: One of the key benefits of family therapy is that it helps individuals see how they are interconnected. Often, each person in a family experiences the same situation very differently, and without a space like family therapy, these differences can lead to misunderstanding, blame, or emotional distance. Through family therapy sessions, each person has the opportunity to share their experience while also learning to listen to others in a more empathetic and grounded way.

blocks.text: Family therapy is especially helpful when communication has broken down. Many families find themselves stuck in cycles of conflict, avoidance, or emotional reactivity. While patterns can feel overwhelming, they are not necessarily fixed for all time. With the support of structured family therapy, it becomes possible to slow these interactions down, examine them more closely, and develop new ways of relating that feel more respectful and connected.

blocks.text: In family therapy, we also explore the roles that each person has taken on within the family system. These roles—such as the caretaker, the peacemaker, the rebel, or the withdrawn one—often develop as ways of coping with stress or unmet needs. While they may have once served a purpose, they can become limiting over time. Family therapy helps bring awareness to these roles so that each individual has more freedom to express themselves authentically, rather than feeling confined to old patterns.

blocks.text: Another important aspect of family therapy is addressing unresolved emotional wounds. Families often carry unspoken pain, whether it stems from past conflicts, misunderstandings, or significant life events. Without a space to process these experiences, they can continue to affect relationships in subtle but powerful ways. Family therapy creates an environment where these emotions can be expressed safely, allowing for healing and reconciliation to take place.

blocks.text: Family Therapy can also support families through major life transitions. Changes such as divorce, remarriage, relocation, illness, or the transition of children into adolescence or adulthood can place significant strain on family relationships. During these times, family therapy provides guidance and stability, helping each member navigate the changes while maintaining a sense of connection and support.

Rather than focusing solely on the child, family therapy looks at the broader context in which these challenges are occurring. This approach often leads to more sustainable and meaningful change, as it addresses the underlying dynamics that contribute to the issues.

blocks.text: Family therapy is not about assigning blame or determining who is right or wrong. Instead, it is about fostering understanding, compassion, and accountability within the family system. Each person is encouraged to take responsibility for their part, while also recognizing the shared nature of relational patterns. This balanced approach helps create a sense of fairness and mutual respect within family counseling sessions.

Over time, this can lead to a deeper sense of belonging and emotional safety within the family.

blocks.text: In our materialistic society, we are socialized to accept the idea that MORE IS BETTER. It is almost as though we are born with this phrase tattooed on our chests. Even as young children we learn that more friends and better grades will be our ticket to approval by our family members and to eventual success in our culture. We believe that the more presents we are given, the more we are loved. We see discrepancies between what we are given and what our siblings are given and we react with concern. We have subtly been learning to measure our worth by what we have and what we do, rather than who we are as unique individuals. We see our parents, who we naturally want to model ourselves after, negotiating for bigger salaries, moving into bigger houses and getting larger SUVs. Clearly, the drive to get more and to "have it all," is a constant source of tension and anxiety in Western culture, especially since the recent economic downturn. We are so entranced by this myth that we go on believing it even in the face of so much evidence to the contrary. We can easily read in the research literature that there is little correlation between children having more toys, adults having bigger and better houses and cars and the overall happiness and satisfaction they each have in life.

blocks.text: Living Apart Together or LAT refers to couples who are in a committed, long-term, monogamous relationship who choose to live in separate dwellings. While the term LAT refers to couples who actually live in separate dwellings, we have come to see that this phenomenon is better understood on a continuum in which partners may arrange their lives to accommodate varying degrees of separation in their lives. On one end of the continuum are couples who have their own space within a shared dwelling, from an office to a private room for meditation to a separate bedroom, or further along the continuum would be a separate floor or wing of the house that was specified solely for one's use. The next level of LAT would be couples who live in a duplex such that each has his or her own full apartment within the larger structure of an apartment building or house. Beyond that, the couple may have their own separate dwellings within five minutes of each other, to a further distance within the same city, to another city, another state, another part of the country, and another continent.

blocks.text: There is no one way to have a relationship. Those of us who are "pursuers" and want to spend more time with our partner are not necessarily more or less healthy than those of us who are "distancers" and want more time and space alone. Each of our positions can be valid and need to be understood and appreciated by our partners. Living situations, whether separate or together, have pros and cons. My hope in writing this article is to increase our awareness of different ways of having relationships so that we can create a form of relationship that works best for each of us, separately and together.
